News will tomorrow publish a dispatch
from Constantinople saying that the Port
has documents, claimed to have been writ
ten by Armenians at Kharput, declaring
the education given by the American mis-
sionaries has seduced their young men
from rectitude and brought calamity upon
them. The dispatch adds that elsewhere
the officials force starving Armenians to
sign papers declaring that the liberty en-
joyed under Turkish rule is not equaled
in any land.


The Daily News will also publish dis
patch from Odessa giving an interview
with Captain Noble of the British steamer
Loeb Rannoch, from Leith November 1
for Odessa, which arrived few days ago
at Chanak, at the entrance of the Dar-
danelles, a few minutes after sundown.
Captain Noble observed that the shore on
either side of the straits was lined with
troops under canvas and that cannon were
placed at close stages along the banks.
Two blank shots, one from each shore,
were fired at the Loeb Rannoch.


The captain did not heave his vessel to,
thinking that the shots were part of some
military maneuver. Soon three shells
were fired at the steamer. The first she'll
dropped under the bow of the steamer, the
second fell astern and the third whizzed
across the bridge few feet from the cap
tain's head.


Captain Noble instantly reversed the
steamers engines. He was astonished
and thought war had been declared be-
tween England and Turkey. Hitherto the
Turkish authorities have always allowed a
time margin for vessels arriving in the
straits after suDdown. The head of the
Dardanelles is covered with torpedoes.


ROME, ITALY, Dec. IA semi-official
telegram from Constantinople says that
the American ad I'm iral who is now at
Smyrna recently asked permission to visit
the Sultan on board his flagship. The re.
quest was refused.

DENVER, CoLo.,. Ocr. 5.-Mrs. Clara
Shortridge-Foltz of San Francisco stopped
off in Denver to-day while en- route home
after a vacation tour abroad. Mrs. Foltz
left for Europe in June. She was accom-
panied by her daughter, Miss Virginia
Foltz, whom she took abroad for the pur-
pose of having her voice tried before
prominent French teachers.


After touring the Continent they at
tempted to cross the English Channel on
the steamer Seaford. When part of the
way across the boat collided with the
freighter Lyon. There were aboard 355
passengers and the Seaford was sunk All
the passengers lost their baggage except
ing what they could carry in hand satchels,
and Mrs. Foltz lost three large trunks
filed with her handsome gowns and bric-a-
brac and treasures which she had picked
up during her tour on the Continent.


Mrs. Foltz was told that she could not
get cent of damages. But the English
officials did not take into consideration
that she was an American woman and
lawyer as we'll, and she went before the
managers of the company and demanded
settlement. She was paid in full for her
property and the payment was promptly
made, too.


''In America railway and steamship
companies are liable for damages in cases
of wreck" said Mrs. Foltz, in speaking of
the matter, land | pointed out that the
English law also covered this important
point. A woman lawyer was something of
revelation to the English officials, and l
have never felt better over any suit that
have won than 1 felt over my victory in
this case"

SPOKANE, WASH, June 25.-Freight-
cars on the Northern Pacific and Great
Northern roads have been systematically
broken and robbed here for the past three
weeks, until thousands of dollars worth of
valuable merchandise has been stolen.
Every effort to locate the robbers has
failed until to-day, when it was learned
that the band was making its headquarters
in dense wood about ten miles north of
the city.


A force of four deputies under Chief
Deputy United States Marshal Vinson
boarded an engine on. the Great Northern
and proceeded to point near where the
robbers were supposed to be. The force was
divided, with instructions to surround the
band, but two of the officers spoiled the
plan of capture by reaching the point too
far ahead of the others. They flushed four
of the band, and running fight took
place in the timber. Over dozen shots
were fired, but no one was hit. The rob-
bers escaped into the brush.


A search disclosed cave near by, full of
stolen goods. The officers are now trailing
the robbers through the woods.

start before telling of the killing. Sheriff
Holcomb received notice of the crime and
a description of the murderer this morn
ing, and Coroner Heating was notified, and
left for the scene tonight.

pounds, is of dark complexion, with a
small mustache and struggling beard.

Juno, Fla, March 11.-William Curry
and John Crawford, young men who have
been spending the winter here hunting,
were attacked by panther yesterday
evening. Curry received wounds which
are thought to be fatal, while Crawford
will lose an eye. The young men were
out hunting and their dog treed young
panther which they shot, and, not sus-
pecting the presence of the mother PAN
ther, the young men laid down their guns
and began work at skinning the animal.


They had hardly begun work when the
mother panther, which was crouching in
the limb, OF tree overhead, sprang upon
them. The hunters were crushed to the
ground and for few minutes were at the
enraged beasts mercy. The animal
planted its claws in the left side of Curry s
face and tore it open. The unfortunate
man rolled over, only to receive another
blow from the razor-like claws. In the
the panther struck him in the right eye,
almost tearing it from the socket; Craw-
ford although in agony and half blinded,
began to strike the beast with his hunting
knife. He dealt it blow after blow, the
fight taking place over Curry's body. :.


Finally the knife found the panther's
heart, and it dropped dead on the uncon-
scious Curry. Crawford was 80 exhausted
that he could not go for assistance, and
the mangled men lay there until night
fall, when they were rescued by another
party of hunters. Curry was found to be
frightfully wounded, and the physicians
say that the stroke which the panther
dealt him across the abdomen will likely
prove fatal. Crawford's principal injury
is the right eye, which will have to be re-
moved. Curry came here from Illinois
and Crawford is from Pennsylvania. The
panther is the largest ever killed on Lake
Worth

PORT TOWNSEND, WASH, Dec. 90
The sealing schooner Willard Ainsworth,
first of the Puget Sound sealing feet to get
started for the seasons work, sails from
here tonight direct for the Japan coast.


She is in charge OF her owners, and they
are taking along extra provisions, which
they expect to sell in the Orient to good
advantage. They go without any hunters
boats.


Captain Crockett says he learned on the
last trip that boats can be purchased in
Japan and sold here on return for double
their cost. Nearly all the sealers from the
Northwest are still flying the British flag,
many such being owned by Americans.


This practice was begun four years ago
when the seizure of Canadian sealers made
the United States Government liable for
damages, whereas American schooners
when seized were promptly confscated
and had no redress.

SEATTLE. WASH, Aug. 26.-Engineer
Neil Mckinley lost his life while at his
post in the wreck of the Great Northern
overland at Richmond Beach last night.
Fireman Barrett jumped from the cab and
escaped with slight bruises. The accident
resulted from running into landslide.


Engineer Mckinley discovered the OBJ
struction on the track ahead in time to
whistle down brakes and reverse the
engine, but the collision came too soon for
him to save his own life. He stood at his
post, and the force of the impact threw
him out of the cab and under the wheels
OF the locomotive, which passed over both
legs above the knees, severing them almost
completely. His left shoulder was also
crushed.


Mckinley was brought to the city late
last night and died at Providence Hospital
early this m orning. He leaves wife and
family. None of the passengers were in
jured. The wrecking crew cleared the
track in few hours and the train pro-
ceeded on its way.

relations. feeling that their property was
not safe while the tramps were in the
vicinity, determined to drive them away.

defiant refusal and the citizens fired in the

were armed, but the citizens returned the
attack and running fight which was kept
lodged behind railroad cars and kept up

posed himself and the fire was returned by
the citizens.


McFeeley and Webster will both die.

Four of the sailors of the California
Yacht Club came near finding an anchor
age at the bottom of the bay yesterday
morning Off Goat Island. Jack Horner
and another yachtsman, of the Stranger,
started to shift ballast from the Stranger
to the Sultana at o'clock in the morning.
The two young salts put 300 pounds of
lead into the Strangers dingy and pushed
off for the Sultana.


They had hardly rowed 100 feet when the
boat capsized and the two men were
thrown into the water. Their cries for
help reached the Seven Bells and Andy
Thorn and Jack Sherry jumped into a
small boat and pulled for the shipwrecked
mariners. Horner and his friend were
pulled into the Seven Bells boat and the
latter set in toward the shore.


Just how the accident occurred nobody
seems to know, but when the dingy was
under the lee of the magazine wharf she
turned over and landed the four men in
the water. The painter got tangled about
Thorn legs and pulled him under. He
struck out for the wharf and managed to
clutch pile, to which he hung for grim
swimmers, and all reached the shore.


Jack Sherry got bowline under Thorn s
arms and moOred him to the pile while
Horner and his friend went for help.


The line about Thorn's legs was cut, and
Thorn was hoisted to the wharf. His legs,
hands, face and body were badly cut, but
he had pluck enough left in him to sail in
yesterdays regatta. The Sultana did not
enter.

PHENIX, ARIz., Nov. 24.-J. T. Hag-
erty, otherwise known as "Sailor Jerry" a
California middle.weight, was knocked
out here tonight by negro known as
Swiftly" a native Arizona fighter, who,
however, has slight reputation in South
ern Colorado and New Mexico.


1t was advertised as fight for points,
but was for blood, lasting but two and
half minutes, during which time ten
kn ockdowns and first blood were recorded.
DR.. Kirkwood, physician here, was
chosen referee. Gus Hirschfeld, a local
sport; G. ?. Bullard, an attorney, and
Barney Hall, were chosen tlmekeepers


1t was evident that something was wrong
with the white man as soon as they en-
tered the ring. At first it was thought the
sailor boy was drunk, but it was deter
mined after the fight that he had nothing
to drink for two weeks. He appeared
groggy, weak in the knees and afraid of
his black opponent. Swiftly however,
seemed confident, and lost no time spar
ing for an opening, but hit straight from
the shoulder. Sailor Jerry, being ratified
and thoroughly scared, left himself un-
guarded and was knocked down seven times
before he reached Swiftly.


Then he dealt him stinging blow in the
face, drawing blood, first bloou. This
seemed to anger the African, who, using
the right-hand swing with terrible force,
Knocked the small but plucky white boy
down again. AS Jerry regained his feet
he caught Swiftly unguarded and struck
out with an upper-cut blow, knocking
down his opponent. This thoroughly
aroused the negro, who, charging like an
infuriated bull, used the terrible right
hand swing again, knocking the white
man out. Jerry remained insensible for
fully an hour. In all not more than thir-
teen blows were dealt.


Corporal Noyes, at one time Jack Demp-
sey's trainer and sparring partner, who
was present, says it was the most remark
able contest he ever saw. Sailor Jerry
weighed about 80 pounds and measured
5 feet 3 inches. Swiftly weighed 1853 pounds
and measured feet 815 inches. About 800
people witnessed the fight.

STANFORD UNIVERSITY, CAL, Nov.
24.-No pleasanter retreat could have been
selected by the Stanford football team than
the little mountain resort where the men
are now located. They are stopping at a
small hotel one mile from Woodside and
about six miles from Redwood City. The
gridiron is surrounded by lofty redwoods
and gigantic oak trees.


The mountain air has wonderfully in
vigorated the men and they have already
increased their eating capacity several fold.
The only fault they find is with the grid
iron itself, which is very dusty, and makes
playing decidedly uncomfortable. The
only spectators at the practice games are q
few ranchmen and small boys from neigh
boring farms, all of whom express wonder
that enjoyment can be extracted from
rolling about in a dusty field for half
day at time in a mad scramble for
leather ball.


Every man went away in roughing
costume, so that very few people would
recognize them back OF Redwood City as
the same fashionably dressed students of
few days previously at Stanford University.


The men will return to college to-
morrow much benefited by their outing
Saturday was spent in hard practice, both
in the morning and afternoon. The play
ers showed the value of pure mountain
air, and worked harder and in better form
than at any previous time. They were
pretty well worn out, however, when night
came.


Reynolds did not play, nor did Frank
enheimer, whose ankle still bothers him.
Fisher and Thomas did good work as half
backs. Weldon is playing fullback, and
Cochran has gone back to tackle. Jeff,
'9S. is being given everv opportunity at
end and has done some remarkable play
ing. Fickert and Carle are both doing
frst-class work as guards.


On Saturday forenoon all the coaches,
including Camp, left for San Francisco to
see the Olympic Reliance game. But
Camp, Downing, Oliver, Walton and Nc
MILAN are expected back to-day to take
charge of the Stanford men.


To-day the players lounged around, get
ting all the rest they could out OF the
twelve hours. There was no signal prac-
tice nor any game. The men were pro-
hibited from taking any long mountain
climbs, so time to-day hung heavy on
their hands.


Neither Captain Cochran nor any of the
men says much about the game with
Berkeley, but they assert that Berkeley
will have job on her hands when she un-
dertakes q walk-over.

PORT HURON, MICH, Nov. 20.-The
steamer J. B. Ketchum and the consort
Montgomery, undertaken, had terrible
experience on Lake Huron last night.
The Ketchum arrived here at noon to-day
in dismantled condition, having jumped
out her masts, rolling in the heavy seas,
smashing her cabin and losing nearly all
of her deckload. The Montgomery broke
away from the steamer during the night
and was driven ashore near Gull Drain,
Ont. She will prove total loss.


The crew of the Canadian schooner
Dauntless was taken off by the tug Crosby
seven miles out from the Fort Gratiot
light. The schooner is at anchor, but is
being battered to pieces by the heavy seas.


POINT EDWARD, ONT, Nov. 2O.-Two
schooners, names as yet unknown, are
ashore about three miles west of Black
well. Tugs have taken the crew off one OF
the schooners. The crew of the other are
in the rigging and the tugs are unable to
reach them.

ASHLAND, Or, June 1.-THE regular
monthly hold-up of the Ager-Klamath
Falls stage occurred last night shortly
after IL o'clock. The robbery took place a
half-mile from Topsy and very near the
scene of the robberies of one month and
two months ago. The same lone high
wayman is supposed to have executed the
job.


The stage left Ager yesterday afternoon,
and when the command to halt came from
ambush Charles Barneburg was driving
with two passengers on board, one of them,
Charles Zwisler, riding outside with the
driver. Zwisler was made to cut open the
letter pouches and throw them out and
the driver told to break open the express
box. The driver told the robber there was
nothing in the box, and the latter seemed
satisfied when he heard it's empty rattle,
and the express box was left intact.


After the coats and vests of all were
thrown out, the robber ordered the driver
to place the stage lantern inside the coach
and move away, and when he finished his
examination they could come back and
get their coats. They moved on fifty
yards, and the robber could plainly be
seen as he went through the registers and
coats, but overlooked some letters and $50
in cash in Zwisler's coat pocket. After
this performance he called the driver and
passengers back to get their clothes and
what was left of the mail. The robber ex-
amined the coach again meantime. Then
he bid the party goodnight and they were
permitted to drive on.


The highwayman was medium size and
wore dark overcoat and light straw hat.
Wore no mask, but kept out of the light
so his features could not be outlined. He
got but few dollars from the passengers,
nothing from the express, and it is thought,
little from the mail pouches.

CONSTANTINOPLE, May 31-Advices
received here from Moosh state that the
dwellings occupied by the French, British
and Russian ENJOYS there have been for
chilly entered by Turkish gendarmes, who
attempted to arrest a servant of the en-
voys. They used abusive language and
were expelled with difficulty. The news,
coupled with the rews from Jeddah that
the British consul and vice consul, the
Russian acting consuls and the French con-
sular secretary were attacked and shot at
outside the town. has caused considerable
excitement in diplomatic circles.


The British vice consul, as already cabled,
was killed. and the British consul was
slightly wounded. The other consular off,
GERS were seriously wounded. The shooting
is attributed to Bedouins.


Three British warships have been ordered
to Jeddah with instructions to protect the
lives of foreigners and to investigate the
killing Of the British vice consul and the
wounding Of the other consular officers.


The Assassination.


JEDDAH, May 31.-The following par
ticulars have been obtained Of the assas-
sination of the British vice consul here
and the wounding of other foreign consular
officers yesterday:


Mr.. w. 8. Richardson, the British con-
sui; the British vice consul, Mr.. Brandt:
the Russian consul. and NJ. D'Orville, the
secretary Of the French consulate. ware
taking a walk together near this town,
when, apparently without any provocation,
they were assailed by eight Bedouin Arabss
Who, when only four yards away from the
consular officers, opened fire upon them
with guns and pistols.


The British vice consul was so badly
wounded that he expired ten minutes after
he was shot While he was lying wounded
on the ground, the Bedouins fired the CON-
tents Of their pistols into him, and also
stabbed him with theif knives. Mr.. Rich
ardson was badly wounded. Mr.. Brandt
had his jaw broken and his nose shot
away. D'Orville alone escaped serious in.
juries. The recovery Of Messrs. Richard
son and Brandt is doubtful.


Fifteen arrests nave been made and the
greatest excitement prevails here, inten-
sified by the fact that several British war;
ships are expected to report shortly, in
order to inquire into the outrage and in
sist upon the punishment of the offenders.


Later reports from the physicians in at
tendance upon the wounded consular off1-
GERS indicate that NJ. D'Orville was much
more seriously wounded than at first ex-
pected. and 1t is feared that he also will
die from his injuries.

Thy voices music, familiar grown
And must leave them all so LON, awhile.
Dear art, farewell, May angels guard thy way

While a great crowd of people was as

laying of the corner stone Of the new st.

temporary floor on which meny Of the peo-

into the basement. One wss killed out

tween thirty and forty others were badly
hurt.


The boards forming the temporary floor
had been laid across the joists, which were
supported in the middle by upright posts.
These suppe rts broke and the floor went
down with crash. Fully 300 people were
thrown into the pit formed by the sagging
in the middle Of the floor.


For moment everybody was paralyzed
by the calamity, but soon there was a rush
forward by those willing to lend assistance
to the crushed and struggling people. This
made matters worse, for fifty more persons
were crowded forward into the hole upon
those who went down with the floor. When
the confusion had subsidized somewhat many
selves did SO by walking and crawling over
their less fortunate companions. The res
cue was begun at once. and all were finally
taken from the pit.

killed. The fatally injured are: Rosa Nc

ling injured internally; Mrs. Kate Died

bers. The contractor was told that the
platform was insecure, but said 1t would
hold all the people that could be crowded
upon it.

continued and the laying Of the corner

ST. JOHNS, N.F., Jan. 8.-A serious lrIot
occurred here to-day, when the crowd of
unemployed workmen resumed their
demonstrations. They hooted the ex-
Premier, Sir William Whiteway, who was
formerly their idol. and then marched to
where the Tourmaline is lying to receive
the captains answer to their petition Of
yesterday.


Captain Sir Richard Poore, the COM
mander. told them the matter was in the
hands of the Government. The crowd
became exasperated and proceeded to the
Minister'S chamber, where the doors were
barred against them. Undaunted, the
crowd set to work to force an entrance,
and doors and windows were soon bat
tered down and ingress gained.


The police attempted to check the work
of destruction, the officers faring badly in
the scuffie that folio owed, and the rioters
were for the time being masters of the
situation. After gaining entrance to the
chamber they found that the members Of
the executive departments were absent.


Later the crowd appealed to the Governor,
but this was also Intellectual. They then
returned to the legislative building, but
they were unable to force an entrance.
They, however. remained on the grounds,
demanding relief and bitterly cursing the
Government.


Hoping to pacify them Prime Minister
Greene appeared and addressed them. He
promised that in two or three days extern
sive public works would be commenced
sufficient to give all employment through
the winter.


His listeners refused to be satisfied with
his promises. and demanded that immedi-
ate relief be furnished. When they were
told that il was impossible to accede to
this demand, the leaders held short con-
ference. and it was decided to attack the
stores on Water street, where large guam
titles Of provisions were supposed TO be
kept.


The first place attacked was Douer's.
The place was soon broken open, but the
mob found no provisions there. Then
attention was turned to Steers store.
which was quickly looted. At this point
armed police intervened and the mob was
driven back at the point of the bayonet


Four men-Bushey. Brown. COady and
King, the prom oters of the riots-were
arrested. The crowd was incliDed to at
tack the police. for the purpose of rescuing
the prisoners. but the officers prevented
this by driving the mob back and then
suddenly closing the gates. The police
are still inside with their prisoners. while
the rioters surround the place, hooting the
officers.


The Tourmaline's marines are under
orders to land should there be any further
outbreak tonight. Special police have
been sworn in and are guarding the other
parts of the city. The Government has
offered to resign, feeling unable to face
the situation.

NEW LONDON, Conn.,, Jan. 26-The ocean
tug Sea King, of Philadelphia, from New
York to Providence, with five coal-laden
barges, put into this port late this morn
ing and reported the loss of her entire tow
and the consequent deaths of thirteen per
sons, including three women and two chill
dren. The drowned are:


From the barge Crocus-Captain Frank
Hoffman, his wife and daughter, and a
deckhapd named Hermac, all of South
Amboy.


From the Albert Mo-Captain Henry
Tucker of South Amboy and Deckhand
Charles Carney of Providence.


From the barge Fadingee-The captain,
his wife and daughter, one deckhand,
names unknown, all supposed to be of
South Amboy.


From the barge American Eagle-Captain
Hartshorn and wife, one deckhand, name
unknown.


Captain w. F. Umpsted of Philadelphia,
who was in charge of the tug, tells this
story:


''We left Wednesday afternoon with five
barges in tow. Race Rock light was passed
Friday afternoon about o'clock with the
weather good and everything favorable for
a good run. Just before midnight a stiff
breeze sprung up from the east and
soon blew up strong southeast gale.
The blow was accompanied by binding
snow gusts, and at 8 o'clock this morning
the tow began pulling and hauling in a
way that indicated trouble.


Cali hands had gathered aft in order to
do something to avert the threatened
catastrophe, but when the three stern
barges broke away and began to founder
we watched them for about half an hour,
all the time struggling to save the tug and
the two remaining barges from destruc-
ton.


''Then the three barges went down. At
6 o'clock the two re eaassfslg barges found
cred and the hawsers from them TO the tug
had to be cut. At great risk the tug was
put about and after repeated efforts lines
were got to men who through the binding
snow could be seen on the barge Nulty,
which still foated. They jumped over
board and were pulled aboard the Sea King
fearfully exhausted.


1.-THE tug unsuccessfully searched for the
others and it was necessary to run for port
to save the tug from the increasing storm.
None of the tugs crew has hope that any
on the barges besides the Hellican and
Purrich survived" )"

The Saturday Pops" which for the past
four and half seasons have entertained
the musical element of San Francisco, are
to be revived again this autumn. There
will be new faces in the orchestra and en-
tirely new programmes, and in the series
of four concerts to be given some works
which have never yet received correct
orchestral Interpretation will be presented.


AS formerly, Sigmund Beel, the violinist,
is managing the concerts, assisted by Mrs.
| Carmichael Carr. They are organized upon
subscription basis, and the artists are only
waiting until $50 subscriptions have been
taken to commence active work. 1t is ex-
pected that the first concert will be givep
in the latter part of September.


| The new people who have been engaged
so far for the regular orchestra are Heine,
Jauleus and Solomon. Solomon will be
second violin, Heine 'celloist and Jauleus
will play the viola. These with Beel and
Mrs. Carr and perhaps one or two more
instruments will compose the regular
orchestra. For special numbers several
additions will be made.


Among the new works which will be
presented will be Brahms sextet for two
violins, two 'celles and two violas,
Dvorak's seXtet for the same, Beethoven'S
septet for two violins, cello, horn, clarionet
and double bass, Svendsen's octet quar-
tet of Semtana and others. The vocal
feature will also be given some promi-
nence, but the solo voices have not yet been
selected.


These concerts have always been ex-
tremely popular with the music-loving
folk of San Francisco, and they have been
the means of introducing many works
which have since been produced all over
the Union. They have always been purely
local. SO far as talent was concerned, and
local music has always been prominent
feature of the programmes. This year
there will be series of four concerts given
this fall, which will bring the total num-
Der given up to forty-eight. 1t is Mr.. Beel's
desire to give a round fifty, and the other
two necessary will probably be given later
on. The concerts are founded on the same
lines as the "Monday Pops" of London,
and they have undoubtedly paved the way
for the symphony concerts which proved
so popular here some time ago. They have
also been the means of developing many
of the local singers, among them G. D.
O'Sullivan and also local composers

King Hum6ert Takes Active Measures


for Relief.


ROME, ITALY, May 21.-Severe earth
quake shocks were experienced yesterday
evening at Sopleto, town situated on a
hill about twenty-four miles north of
Rieti. Much damage has been done and
many houses were destroyed. Assistance
has been sent to Sopleto from Rieti, and
everything possible will be done torelieve
the sufferers. The damaged town has a
population of 1000.


The dispatches from Florence show that
the authorities there are doing everything
possible to repair the damage done by the
earthquake of Saturday. Troops have been
employed ever since the disaster succoring
the suffering in the neighboring towns and
villages, and the distress has consequently
been greatly lessened.


King Humbert has from the first, by his
special request, been kept informed re-
garding the extent of the disasters and the
measures OF relief, and has personally di-
rected the operations of the military au-
thorities. He is understood to have sub
scribed literally from his private purse for
the relief of the destitute.

from Denver, Colo, says:


1t is feared that a party of Princeton
students have fallen into the hands of the
Bannock Indians. Nearly two weeks ago
the students forming the geological expe-
dition went through Union Pass, and since
telegrams have been received for them
without affording any means of delivery.

and due on their return trip about the end
of July. They are in a dangerous country,
and if they are alive the fact remains that
the Government has recently stirred to
great activity, as orders were received
yesterday at Fort Washakie for the send
ing of troops. There are only forty-three
men at the post, and the expedition can
not be very formidable, but it is the best
that the army can do.

there are fully 800 Indians assembled there
and of the number there are fifty Sho-

forcibly detained by the Bannocks and

The damage to the city is fifty buildings

With these losses must be added the

The Magdalena branch of the Santa Fe

The water washed away the main track

waves, one filling the arroyo over bankfull

Some statistics have been published here
concerning the fatal accidents which have
occurred in the Alps during the year 1894.
Up to the present time the number of fatal
accidents reported is thirty-three, whereas
the average number during late years
amounted to forty-one. Among these thirty
three cases three were caused by lightning,
from which no death had been reported
for decades in the records of Alpine climb
ing. Two tourists met their deaths by the
fall of avalanches, two through the descent
of heavy stones, Miss Davidson, the daugh-
ter of an English vicar, being one of the
victims. Six persons died from exhaustion
after snowstorms, exposure to cold and bad
weather. Fourteen lost their lives by miss
ing their footing and falling down preci-
pices, six from pursuing dangerous paths,
and the other eight in the course of com
paratively easy climbing. One tourist fell
down glacier fissure and another was lost
while seeking edelweiss. Besides these
thirty-three cases, four deaths are unex-
planned, among them that of an English
man and his guide near Cortina, in the
Ampezzothal, Southern Tyrol. = Vienna

The treacherous tides which swirl around
the North Head almost opposite Fort
Point came very near claiming another
victim last night in the lumber schooner
G. T. Hill. The vessel left here about $50
o'clock, and stood out through the Golden
Gate under easy sail. There was but lit
tie wind blowing, but the tide was running
very strong on the ebb.


Soon after passing Fort Point the wind
died away almost completely, and then the
swift tide took the vessel in its clutches
and began to drive it upon the rocks close
to where the Inflated steamer New York
went ashore.


Captain Forrest, realizing the danger
which threatened the craft, had both
anchors thrown over, and fortunately they
"caught" Just as the schooner was about to
strike. She swung in broadside with the
tide, however, and her stern grazed the
rocks. Signals were sent up in the shape
of skyrockets, and the people at the Point
Bonita Lighthouse, who saw the position
of the vessel, also sounded the siren five
times, which is a signal for assistance.


The information about the perilous
situation of the schooner was telephoned
to the Merchants Exchange and the tug
boat offices. The tugboats Active and
Hercules at once sped out to the scene, the
tug ActiVe OF the SpreckelS line arriving
first and making fast to the schooner with
hawser. Between the two tugs the
schooner was hauled out from her position
of danger, although there was some time
spent in clearing her anchors, which had
fouled with the sunken rocks, and shortly
after midnight they brought her into port
once more.


Captain Mcconnell of the United States
revenue boat Hartley also deserves credit
for going out to the scene of the supposed
disaster as soon as the first danger rocket
sped skyward. The G. I. Hill is owned by
II. G. LASER of this city, and has been in
the lumber business since 1885, She was
but little injured by the few bumps which
she had again st the rocks

| London. Jan. 3O.-The North German Lloyd
steamship Elbe bound from Bremen for New
York. sunk in a collision with small

morning She carried 400 people. Only twenty

In a pitiable condition. The passengers were
but half clothed Their few garments were
frozen stiff. their hair was coated with ice.

completely. The officers and sailors were fully
dressed but their clothes had been drenched
and frozen and they had been almost paralyzed
with cold and fatigue. They had been ashore

ficiently to tell the story oe the wreck. Their

The Elbe left Bremen Tuesday afternoon.
The few hours of the voyage before the disas-
ter were uneventful. At o'clock this morning
the wind was blowing hard and tremendous
sea was running. The morning was unusually
dark Numerous lights were seen In all direc-
tions, showing that many vessels were nearby.
The captain ordered. therefore. that rockets
should be sent up at regular intervals to warn
the craft to keep out of the Elbe's course.


A CRASH IN THE DARKNESS.
II was near to o'clock and the Elbe was
some fifty miles off Lowestoft. coast OF Suffolk.
when the lookout man sighted a steamer OF about
l50O tons approaching. He gave the word and.
as precaution, the number OF rockets was
doubled, and they were sent up at short intervals
The warning was without effect. The steamer
came on with unchecked speed. and before the
EIbe could change her course or reduce her speed
notably there was the terrific crash OF the COL
lison.


The Elbe was hit abaft her engine-room. When
the smaller steamer wrenched away an enormous
hole was left in the Elbe's side. The water
poured through and down into the engine-room
in cataract The room filed almost instantly.
The engines were still and the big hulk began TO
settle.


The passengers were in bed. The bitter cof
and rough sea had prevented any early risins
and none except the officers and crew on duty
was on deck when the ship was struck. The
shock and crash reused everybody. The steerage
was in n panic In a moment. ana men, women
and children. half dressed or In their night
clothes came CTOWulHB uP thS SSAAb~'~-- ''~'
They had heard the sound Of rushing water as
the other steamer backed off. and had felt the
Elbe lurch and settle They had grasped the
fact that 1t was then life or death with them, and

They clung together in groups, facing the cold
and storm. and cried aloud for help or prayed on

THE LIFEBOATS LAUNCHED.

Princeton for the first time since 1889 The
last time these teams came together on the
''gr:diron' six years ago much bad feeling
resulted, and Princeton's victory was mar
red by the charges of rough play brought
against them by the Harvard sympathizers.
The breach was wide one, too, and all
efforts to bring the teams together again
failed until this fall, when Harvard S
sauabble with Yale paved the way for
reunion, and the two old enemies have now
buried the hatchet and smoked the pipe of
peace.


Both teams have been training hard for
the event, and each will play all the tricks
it's players know before time is called, de-
spite the fact that coaches from both Yale
and the University of Pennsylvania will
be watching every move as closely as so
many ferrets. Princeton will meet Yale
three weeks later in New York. and Har-
ward will play Pennsylvania in Cambridge
the same day.


Princeton began this falls foot ball work
with few of last years veterans, though
among the substitutes of 1894 there were
many promising men who did not graduate
in the spring. "Beefy' Lea, last years
crack tackle was chosen to guide the for
tunes Of the team this year. and he has
proved both popular and efficient as captain
and coach.


The Princeton men have met with about
the usual number of accidents among the
candidates for their team. In the center of
the line Princeton is nearly as strong this
fall as last. The absence of Wheeler from
left guard will make a hole He is coach
ing Riggs, last years center, to fill his
place at left guard. and Rhodes, the vet
eran right guard, will probably fill the
same position again this fall. For the CEN
ter a new man had to be trained


Captain Lea is certainty for right tackle,
while Church, one of last years substi-
tutes, will probably fill the same position
on the other side of the line. Cochrane,
also a substitute last year. will probably
play on one end while Johnston, Knight
and three or four others are trying for the
other end.


Behind the line, Princeton has many
promising candidates, but most of them are
new men. Pope, who played full back for
the University of Virginia, is perhaps the
best kicker among those trying for full
back, though Barnard and Baird are both
strong aspirants for the disputed place.
Armstrong is perhaps the most brilliant of
all the backs.


The Princeton players have had the bene-
fit this fall of a great deal of expert coach
ing by veteran Princeton players.


While most of Harvard's rush line is COM
posed of new men, she is particularly for
tunate in having so many of her last years
backs in college to play again this fall The
absence this fall of Bob Wrenn, the clever
little quarter back, is the only important
vacancy behind the line, and there are sew
eral men who promise to fill his shoes ac-
ceptably. Wrenn himself is coaching the
candidates for this position, and Borden for
Beale will probably pass the ball for Har-
ward In both her two big games Confer
man is the star half back of the team, and
is almost sure of his place, while Charles
Brewer will probably fill the other position
For full back Harvard will depend on Fair
child, last years kicker, or Dunlop.


in Harvard there seems to be a dearth of
heavy men, and the crimson will have to
depend on Doucette and Jaffray, two new
men, and Holt. an experienced player, for
the guards. Capt. Arthur Brewer will un-
doubtedly play right end. while Newell will
probably fill the other end of the line.


Harvard has been practcng a number of
new tricks under the altered rules, and
some innovations may be expected from the
acknowledged men in tomorrows game


The difference between the playing rules
under which the games of Harvard and
Princeton will be played in other cases has
caused compromise to be reached which
will alter slightly the rules of each on this
occasion. The changes, however, are all
technical ones. and the game remains the
same to the ordinary observer.


Great preparations have been made at
Princeton for this big game, and a large
ed upon the Princeton field which will ac-
ccmmodate about 10000 people, and special
trains will be run from New York and Phila-
delphia to accommodate the great crowd
from both cities that will go to see the game.
No big game has taken place in Princeton
before since 1886, and this fact, coupled
with the old rivalry between Harvard and
Princeton, and their long separation, should
greatly add to the attendance.

PLYMOUTH, England, Sept. l9.-1he
steamer Beresford has arrived here hav-
ing in tow the Vulture and four ships
boats containing the captain and passen-
gers of the Netherland Steamship com
pany's steamship Edam OF Rotterdam,
from New York, bound for Amsterdam.
At O'Clock this morning the Edam col
lided with the Turkistan', IN dense fog.
The Edam foundered and the Turkistan
was lost to view IN the fog. The captain.
passengers and crew OF the Edam, who
took to boats i'm ediatly after the coils
ion, were picked up by the Traveller.


The trawler Vulture was on the fishing
grounds fifteen miles from Eddystone
lighthouse last night. Just before L
o'clock thick fog came up. Those on
the vulture heard a great blowing OF
whistles, then terrific crash. The Vul-
ture i.m sdiateiy went alongside the
steamship Edam, which was rapidly fill
ing. Captain Brunsma requested the
Vulture to stand by. The ships boats
were quickly lowered and passengers
helped into them without accident. The
passengers were greatly alarmed, but
there was no panic. A majority went,on



men and children were first mbarked in
the ships boats. The sea was perfectly
smooth. TIE Tnrkistan: which did not
acpear to have sustained injury by the
collision, stood by until danger had
passed, then proceeded in the direction
OF Cardiff. The Edam founderei at 3
O'Clock, two hours after the collision.


The Edam and Turkistan came together
with great force, although proceeding
cautiously in the fog. The Turkistan $
PROV made great hole III the side OF
the Edam. Both vessels Immediately
lowered boats and many passengers were
transferred from the Edam by the Turk
fstan's boats. Another account says the
Edam foundered within half an hour
after the collision. Everything is being
zone at Plymouth TO make the ship
wrecked people comfortable, and supply
them with clothing. as all their baggage
was lost. The Edam carried ninety-three
steerage passengers. The Turkistan' s
bows were badly damaged.


The steamer Edam was built at hotter
dam in 1858. Shs was $50 feet long, 80
feet beam, % feet deep. She registered
3l30 tons gross, 1867 tons net.


The Edam was struck amldshlps on the
port side, Captain Brunsma being on the
bridge at the time. He had heard the
Turkistan whistle and had replied sew
eral times. When at last the vessel
doomed up in the fog it was too late to
avoid a collision, but the captain imme-
diately signaled to reverse the engin as
and ordered everybody on deck. He
directed that the passengers and crew be
divided into four parties, one for each OF
the steamships boats. The boats were
lowered without any panic. The women
and children were handed down into
them, some of them but half dressed. In
the meantime boats from the Turkistan
had arrived and Captain Drew of the
Vulture from Brixham, who had heard
the crash, brought his trawler alongside
the fast sinking Edam.


Captain Drew OF the Vulture in an in
terview with representative of the As
ISOLATED Press, said that he had Just
reached the fishing grounds, about fifteen
miles. northwest of the Eddystone light
house, when the fog bank came up.
Hearing the sound of whistling and
little later the crash, he bore immediate
ly down on the noise. The night was so
dark that he was unable to see how large
the vessels were or where the Turkistan
struck the Edam. He did not thinksthat
the Turkistan was much damaged but be
ascertained that her stem was somew hat
injured.


The officers of the Edam refused to give
any details of the disaster beyond saying
there was no panic on board the steam
ship but that every body kept perfectly
cool. From other sources it was learned
that the steamer settled down at the stem
first and sank in about forty minutes
after the vessels struck, by which time
all the boats had got clear of the doomed
ship. Captain Brunsma tried to board
her again before she sank, but the dau-
ger was too great. The passengers were
all emlgrants of the poorest class and
none of them could speak English.


When they reached Plymouth they pre-
scented pitiable spectacle, the most for
tunate of them being only half clad :.
They were, however, soon provided with
clothing. English yachtsmen contribut-
ed money for the alienation of their dis
tress and local tradesmen gave generously
for the same purpose.

The Chinese god of war was made to bite
the dust last night in more places than
one, while Mortified highbinders looked on
in amazement. 1t was the grand inaug-
uration of New Year festivities in China
town. The streets were bright with COL
ored lanterns and the pungent odor of
burning punk assembled from hundred
shrines. Every nook and corner was
packed with Mongolians and white visitors,
and the many highbinders were preparing
for veritable harvest of blackmail and its
inevitable accompaniment in Chinatown
murder.


In seven places these outlaws were
gathered. Some of them had built affairs
and enthroned idols decked with grotesque
metal ornaments, urns and gorgeous orien-
tai embroideries. Only the war god, the
fierce unconquerable hero who presides
over the destinies of all belligerent Chinese,
was thus honored by them, but hardly
were the affairs finished before squads of
policemen with axes in hand dashed in
and demolished them.


This wholly unexpected action of the po-
lice created CONSERVATION among the bind
ers. Sergeant Gillian and his men made
similar raid about ten days ago when in
formed by Chinese merchants that unless
prompt measures were taken to suppress
the desperadoes an outbreak might occur
any day before the present festive time came
to close. Several signs and insignia of
the highbinders were then confiscated. Ser
geant Gillian was told early yesterday that
the respectable element of Chinatown was
greatly excited by an influx of well-known
highbinders from Stockton and Fresno.


81 received notification" said the SER
geant, "that gangs of desperate characters
had arrived and systematic blackmail of
merchants was in order. The object was
to support several highlander societies. So
made an investigation quietly and found
that the highbinders had hung out signs
and opened headquarters. I also saw
enough to convince me that these fellows
meant business"


The police waited for night to come be-
fore making simultaneous raid on the
Ratchet mems headquarters. Policemen
McManus, Lynch and Ellis raided the
Dock Tin Tong, at $40 Clay street, and cap
tured war joss, which the Mongols tried
to hide. The altar, code of laws and other
paraphernalia were confiscated. AZ 35
Waverly place the Say Teen Tong resort
was broken into and denuded of its signs
and papers. The Hig Sig highbinders, at
70l Spofford alley, were next raided.


At the same time Sergeant Gillian and
Policemen Tuite and Duane surprised the
Sam Ducks at Ross alley, the Ben On
Tong at S15k Jackson street, the Wah
Ting Sang Tong at 1913 Dupont street, and
the Kai Sen Shea Tong at 819% Washing
ton street. The Kai Sen Shea highbinders
had an elaborate josshouse. Their affairs
were decorated with costly metal vessels,
vases and candlesticks and draped with
magnifcently embroidered silks, and all
around were condemnatory pictures and
signs in frames.


While the police were gathering up every
thing portable the highbinders hid their
war god beneath an ebony table. But the
police knew from experience that it breaks
the spirit of the ruffians to carry off the
joss and hunt for the god followed. A
howl of imprecations burst from the mad
dened outlaws when the joss was found
and confscated.


| No more desperate society exists in
Chinatown than this same Kai Sen Shea,
which. the police say, has a bad record.
The Ben On Tong is similarly dreaded by
the peaceable Chinese, for its Ratchet men
bear reputation for absolute disregard
| for life and law.

SANTA CRUZ. Dec. 9.--Ten days ago
Fred Markham, hackman in this city,
received letter stating that his mother
had died in Battle Creek, Mich, as the re-
suit of railroad accident, and that the
remains would be inferred before he could
reach Battle Creek. where he formerly re-
sided. A few days later he was astonisheti
at receiving another letter containing in
formation that his mother was alive and
would probably recover. The let
ter further stated that his
mothers apparent death had &C.
cured when the first letter was written.
Arrangements for her burial we're then
under way, but while the funeral services
were in progress, the minister, relatives
and congregation were terrified by sound
from the coffin, and were almost paralyzed
with surprise when, a moment later, the
coffin lid was broken and Mrs Markham
was found to be alive. 1T appears that she
had suffered from conclusion of the brain
and for two days was unconscious, the cur
rent of life only returning short time be-
fore interment.

| EUREKA CAL, July 1S.-This morning
was almost entirely given over to the re-
ception of visitors, of whom about 10000
had arrived before noon.


Shortly before 1 O'Clock the great crowd
assembled before the pavilion, where
Queen Sequoia was to receive her crown.
The Queen, accompanied by her nine
lovely maids arrayed in white, soon ap-
peared, guarded by her six mounted
knights in armor and accompanied by her
prime minister, and assembled the throne.
The path which led to the pavilion was
thickly strewn with flowers, tribute of the
fiower-girls.


After the Mayor in a beftting speech
had presented Queen Sequoia with the keys
of the city and Prime Minister Puter had
delivered the royal proclamation the reti-
nue. entered their respective vehicles and
made haste to join the grand parade,
which was in course of formation about
the courthouse block


The Queens dress was of green satin,
embelished with pearls. The robe, which
was three yards in length, was carried by
liveried pages. 1t was OF garnet colored
velvet and trimmed with ermine.


The parade was the grandest affair ever
witnessed before in Redwood Realm"
and compared favorably with other like pa
rades previously seen in the State. 1t was
composed of four divisions, commanded
by the marshal and his aids. Floats rep
resenting industries and private enter
prises, decorated carriages, uniformed So
cieties, fire companies and the Chief and
officers of police made up the parade. The
floats were by far the grandest and most
interesting feature. No expense was
spared in their construction, and the origi-
nality and ingenuity displayed were aston
ishing.


The water fete which took place on the
bay this evening was fitting termination
to the pleasures of the day. The process
sion formed on the water at $3.50. Steam
ers, launches yachts and rowboats, dec
GRATED with japanese lanterns and lighted
with red and blue lights, presented the
grandest sight ever seen on Humboldt Bay.
a miniature of the Philadelphia, rugged
and blazing with illuminations, was an
object of much admiration. The process
sion was led by Admiral Curly in the
Antelope. Following came the Queens
barge, built in the shape of swan.


When about half a mile down the bay
the flagship and the Queens barge turned
and, as they returned up the bay, re-
viewed the magnificent and highly illu-
minated procession amid general saluting.

CHICAGO, ILL, July 23.-Dynamite in
stantly killed three men and seriously in
jured a fourth, on the drainage canal at 2
o'clock this afternoon. The accident took
place near Willows Springs, and was
caused by a premature explosion during
the process of tamping.


The dead are: William Kelly, 80 years
old, lived in Marquette, Mich; Thomas
Somker. 40 years old, lived on Wood street,
Chicago; Joseph Smith, 80 years old, resi-
dence unknown.


Injured: Matthew Healy, 80 years old,
severe scalp wounds, will recover.


The men were employed as laborers on
section 2, for Macarthur Bros. contrac-
tors. Nearly 100 men were working a
short distance away, and it is remarkable
that more deaths did not result.


AT the time of the explosion the men
were pounding dynamite sticks into hole.
Suddenly there was deafening explosion,
the rock beneath them shot up and the
three men were hurled high into the air
and fell over twenty yards from the point
of the explosion, mangled almost beyond
recognition. The gangs of men became
panic-stricken and ran for their lives.
Healy was hit by huge piece Of rock and
rendered unconscious.


The cause of the explosion is mystery
to the men employed about the canal,
nothing of a similar nature having &C.
Cured there before.

NEW YORK, n. Y, July 23.-The Nor
wegian steamer Terrier arrived from
Demerara this morning, and reports that
on July IL, outside the harbor of Deme-
rara, she collided with the schooner Eagle
of Barbados and sunk her. Twenty-four
persons were saved and five lost. Those
lost were two women, one child and two
men.


When the schooner was struck among
the first to aband on her was the captain,
who did nothing whatever to assist the
passengers, among whom were several
women and children. He walked the
steamers deck sobbing, moaning and
wringing his hand.


All the men abandoned the vessel with
out attempting to assist the women or
children. After the accident the sea was
covered with all kinds of floating material
from the wreck. The search was contin-
ued for long time in the hope that some
unfortunates would be found clinging to
the wreckage, but none were found. The
Terrier returned to port, landed the people
of the Eagle and proceeded on her vow
age. The Terrier sustained slight damage.

Los ANGELES, March 8.-Three of the 400
little orphan girls who attended the citrus
fair this afternoon upon the invitation of
the managers are lying in the hospital
bruised and injured, the victims of run
away accident.


The Catholic Sisters had conducted safely
their long line of small charges to the pa
vllion, and had started on the return trip.
An electric car was waiting on Broadway
for load of passengers, and the girls were
Just beginning to find seats aboard when
runaway horse came tearing down the
street The animal was going at terrific
rate of speed and dragged behind him a
two-wheeled cart. The crowd of children
filled the street completely, and before the
pedestrians on the sidewalk could give
warning the horse and cart were through
the line of girls.


Susie Brussuille, aged seven years, was
thrown high in the air, and landed on the
hard pavement, heap of bruised flesh
and broken bones. Leonita Teaver aged
eight years, and Virginia Morillo, aged
ten, were knocked down and trampled
underneath the hoofs of the frightened
horse, which continued its mad course down
the street until it collided with the tele-
phone post and was secured.


All of the injured children are still alive
but grave fears are entertained for the re-
covery OF any of them. The sad accident
spoiled the holiday for the orphans, and
the little ones talk in mournful whispers
at the asylum tonight.

KANSAS CITY, Mo-, April 8.-The rail
roads in Western Kansas and Eastern Colo
RADIO have been battling since last Friday
night with combination of sand and snow
storms which swept over these regions
completely demoralizing train schedules
and causing serious inconvenience and dis
comfort to travellers.


The particles of snow and sand were
driven across the prairies at terrific speed
by the gale, and many are reported to
have been suffocated by the whirling
clouds of sand. Railroad cuts were filled
up and tracks buried completely. The
snow melted and the sand settled down in
hard, unyielding mass. Rotary snow
plows were practically useless against this
new enemy and the railroad companies
were compelled to engage men with pick:
aud shovels to remove the sand from the
tracks.


While the gale was in progress the sui
fering of the workmen was intense. On
board the belated trains the condition o.
the traveller was not much better. The
sand sifted in persistently until the floors
of the cars were covered, and the air in the
cars became hot and sitting. The pas
sengers in several instances were com
PEELED to go without food.


The first train since Friday to reach
this city from Denver, except the Burling'
ton trains, was the Missouri Pacific train
which arrived yesterday. The Burling
tons tracks were outside the storm belt.


The Union Pacific did not bring in 6
single train from Denver until O'Clock
this evening.


No Rock Island trains from the west had
reached here, up to o'clock this evening
since Saturday.


No direct wires were secured to Denver
until this morning, the telegraph com
panies being compelled to send their bust
ness for Denver and points beyond via the
Northern route.


Cattle on the ranges have suffered great
hardships, and robably considerable loss
was sustained by the stockmen.

killed. The rest commenced to retreat,
pursued by the bandits, who killed many.

bayoneted.

the firing, went to the rescue of their COM
rades. but the rioters prepared an ambush
for them, into which they were easily led
and from which it is believed only ten es-
capped. The rioters claim that their loss
was insignificant.

ants were only bandits and small in num-
bers, while others claim that this force
combined five small revolutionary bands,
who united. They recognize no leader,
and are only opposed to the Gutierrez
regime.

AUSTIN, TEX, Nov. 6.-The weather
was fine to-day and large attendance
saw the regatta races. The great event of
the day was the final heat of three miles
with turn, double scuIl, for the worlds
championship and a purse of $1,000 be-
tween England's cham pions, Bubear and
Barry. and Americas flyers, Teemer and
Rogers. Both crews were in the pink of
condition, and the course, with gentle
south breeze blowing over it, was all the
sportsmen could desire.


The start was made in excellent style,
Teemer and Rogers taking water slightly
ahead. Bubear and Barry followed, and a
few sweeping strokes sent them ahead OF
the Americans, and as they passed the
first quarter stake a full boats length of
daylight was between them. The Ameri-
cans were pulling straight up the course,
sticking to their oars at thirty-eight clip.


AT the three-quarter stake the English
were only half boats length ahead.
Bubear and Barry were evidently not
alarmed and pulled away with beautiful
stroke. The Americans continued to gain
on them, and both crews rounded the
mile and half flag together.


Down the homestretch they were neck
and-neck. At the three-quarter stake the
English had forged ahead about half a
boats length. The Americans again
spurted, and as they neared the last quar-
ter flag the boats were about even, and
kept that way until within an eighth of a
mile of the home line. At this point Bu-
bear and Barry spurted, and, with a fifty
five stroke, crossed the finishing line at
least a couple of boats lengths ahead. The
official time was 17:40, which breaks the
worlds record of Is :02.


The second event was single scull trial
heat, three miles, with three turns, four
times over the course, between J. Gaudaur,
Hanlan, Peterson, Rogers and Teemer
Peterson led off, with Rogers second. 1t
was steadily pulled and pleasing race,
with several changes in the relative po-
sitions of boats until the last stretch was
reached. In the last turn of the stake
Gandaur led, Rogers second, Peterson
third. Teemer had dropped out and on
the home dash Hanlan pulled out, leav-
ing Gaudaur, Rogers and Peterson to
finish, and they crossed the line in the
order named. Time, 1914.

BRUSSELS, BELGIUM, Oct. Two
trains collided between Wavre and Ottig-
nies. Both trains were wrecked. Eighteen
persons were killed outright and one hup-
dred were injured, some fatally. Among
the passengers were Fl. Beernaert, Presi-
dent of the Chamber of Deputies, and his
wife and sister. Nine. Moulon, the latter,
was killed.


Later news of the accident near Wavre
shows that the disaster was a great deal
more serious than the first report indi-
Gated. 1t is now known that eighteen per-
sons were killed outright and over 1OC
badly injured. Many of these were so
badly hurt that they cannot live.


The collision was not between two pas
senger trains, as first reported, but be-
tween passenger and freight trains. The
engine of the freight train struck the pas.
senger- cars, which were crowded with pas
sengers. Two of the cars telescoped and a
third was thrown upon and fell on them
crushing the passengers in a trightful way


The rescuing party worked throughout
the night taking out the dead and injured
from the wreckage.


The accident is attributed to the absence
of the regular signal man at Ottignies
who had been replaced by man having
an imperfect knowledge of the device.

SAN DIEGO, CAL, April 1s-An Italian,
known only as Antonio, was killed and
robbed on the railroad, between Oceanside
and Vista, Just after dark last night.


The murdered man had been seen with
two Italians and an American walking
from Escondido, where he had been work
ing on an irrigation ditch and had just
been paid off.


His three companions appeared at Ocean
side this morning and said they were
walking on the track single file, Antonio
in the lead, when man jumped out from
a culvert where he had been lying in wait
and fired, wounding Antonio. He fired
second time, the bullet striking the
wounded man in the breast, killing him
instantly. The others ran away.


They said it was too dark to identify the
murderer, and one of them declared that
man on horseback had chased him some
distance. The men say that they returned
to the spot this morning and found An
tonio's body. All his money was gone.


Three men were arrested at Oceanside
and charged with the murder.


The body was placed under guard await
ing the Coroner, who went up tonight.
with Deputy District Attorney Kirby. The
latter received information which tended
to confirm the suspicious that the three
men killed their companion for the purpose
of robbery. An inquest will be held to-
morrow.

The big ferryboat Solano was towed down
from Port Costa yesterday by the tug Res
cue and locked at Oakland long wharf for
repairs. The vessel has been plying be-
tween Port Costa and Benicia for MANY
years, carrying trains to and fro. and is
perhaps one of the best-known craft of her
kind in the world.


Last week one set of her engines broke
down completely, and she has been brought
here to be thoroughly renovated, over
hauled and repaired. How long this work
will take is not known. While the vessel
is laid up the overland train will travel
over the Stockton route, and passengers
from the Suisun and Sacramento valleys
will come down by way of Vallejo, there
being no vessel on the bay fitted to take
the Solano's place.

text:
A Venerable Side-wheeIer Which Has


Seen Much Service.


One more round trip of the Mirimichi
between Montreal and the gulf ports and
the stanch old boats life work will have
ended The quaint side.wheeIer of the
fashion of generation ago will give place
to the modern twin-screw steamship Cam
pagna, which is even now on her way down
the canal. The early history of the Miri-
michi is unique, inasmuch as she was de-
signed for an entirely different trade
since the early '70's. She was built
at London, England, in 1864, by ].
Penn, and was christened the
Teaser For whom she was orig
inally built is not known. This was kept
secret, no doubt, for the reason that her
intended trade was of a semi-piratical ma
ture. She was designed for blockade
runner between Southern ports of the
United States and Europe. In that year,
1864, the War of the Rebellion was at its
height and the navy of the United States
had completely blocked all traffic between
the rebel ports and Europe. The speed of
the Teaser was about sixteen miles per
hour, which was accounted very fast in
these days, and it was thought that she
could outsail the ships of the United States
navy. She was captured, however, on her
first trip, as she was trying to get out of
blockaded Southern port with a cargo of
cotton. After the close of the war in 1865
she was sold by the United States Govern
ment, and for time was employed in the
Gulf of Mexico between New Orleans and
Galveston. Coal being very expensive,
this did not prove paying investment and
she was laid up in New Orleans until 1872,
when her present owners, the Quebec
Steamship Company, purchased her. AL
terations, such as the Lighthouses, etc.,
have since been made. Her boiler were
renewed six years ago, though the engines
are the same as when she was built. She
has made 300 round trips to the lower
ports. which aggregate over 100000 miles,
and in all her service has never lost life
Montreal Star.

continued the shooting. Corcoran's pistol

emptied. Then LAVA wheeled and run

The Pearsons will case, which has
been pending before Judge Coffey, has
been finally decided and as far as the SUI
perior Court is concerned, it is settled.
Judge Coffey has granted petition from
Mr.. Boone, attorney for the Valentines and
Wheelers, cousins of the testator, that all
property which descended to Hiram Ar
thur Pearsons from his father be divided
among the descendants of Mrs. Lucy A.
Valentine and Mrs. Clarissa P. Wheeler,
and that all property bequeathed to the
testator from his mother, Ann Charity
Pearsons (nee Mathewson) be divided
among the five Mathewson claimants, or
their representatives.


Hiram Arthur Pearsons was the son of
Hiram Pearsons, whose father was Parker
Pearsons. Parker Pearsons married first
Emma Bartlett, and after her death he
married her sister, Polly Bartlett. Mrs.
Lucy A. Valentine was the daughter of
Emma Pearsons and Mrs. Clarissa Wheeler
and Hiram Pearsons, the testator's father,
were children of Polly Pearsons. Hiram
Pearsons married Ann Charity Mathew
son. and the testator was the issue of this
marriage. Ann Mathewson had five
brothers and sisters, and their representa-
tives constitute the Mathewson claimants.


Mrs. Valentine and Mrs. Wheeler, aunts
of the testator, were his nearest relatives
on his fathers side, and they, or as they
are now dead, their heirs-at-law, will re-
ceive all the property acquired by the tes-
tator from their common ancestor, Hiram
Pearsons. This amounted to about five
sixths of the inherited estate. On the other
hand the brothers and sisters of Ann
Charity Mathewson were his nearest kin
on his mothers side, and they will receive
the remaining one-sixth, which came to
the testator from his mother. The prop
erty which Pearsons HIMSELF acquired dur
ing his life will be divided into seven equal
heirs. Where one of these original heirs is
dead his or her share will be divided
among the heirs of the deceased heir.

A crowd considerably smaller than usual
was attracted to the park yesterday after
noon. The weather was anything but
pleasant, on account of heavy fogs that
began to roll in about P. NJ, but still this
did not keep the regular Sunday visitors
away. The amusement places and main
avenues were comfortably filled with
strollers and vehicles of all kinds, from the
stately family coach to the speedy bicycle.


The excellent musical programme which
the park band rendered attracted many
who ordinarily seek pleasure in long strolls
or In some quiet corner. From the OPEN
ing number until Spadina waved his baton
through the last piece, it WAS almost i'm
possible to secure a seat within comfort
able distance of the band stand.


The cold winds and the heavy fogs did
not prevent the little children from turn
ing out in force. While there have been
days when the little ones were more nu-
merous than yesterday. there were anite
enough on hand to keep the donkeys
busy, and as for the merry-go-round it was
almost impossible to find vacant seat
any time from to o'clock.


The wheelmen were out in great num-
bers, and they doubtless found the after
noon more to their liking than the thou
sands of pedestrians, or those who ,lolled
on the soft cushions of carriages.


When the concert was over nearly 300
cyclers gathered on the circular course
near the band stand, and for nearly an
hour spun noiselessly over the course,
while occasionally some rider more daring
than the rest would resort to little fancy
riding, to the delight of the assembled
thousands. There were any number of
tandems out, and 'bloomer" riders were to
be seen on all sides.


There were very few visitors at the Cliff
House yesterday, owing to the cold, biting
winds and fogs. The only event out of the
ordinary was the hundreds of thousands of
Spanish ssmen-of-war" that came in with
each wave. For while this unusual sight
afforded amusement to old and young
alike though it was not long before the
offensive odor drove the pleasure-seekers
from the beach.

MADRID, SPAIN, June 5.-Captain
Clavigo, who shot and seriously wounded
Captain General Prima Ribera after the
latter had refused him the hand of his
daughter on Monday, was shot to-day, he
having been sentenced to death by court
martial. He displayed marvellous forti-
tude and composure.


Captain Clavigo walked to the prison
van smoking cigarette and bowed to the
crowd assembled within the prison gate.
They acknowledged his courtesy by cheer
ing loudly for the captain. The prison
van, surrounded by gendarmes, proceeded
to the square of San Isadore, on the bank
of the Manzanares River. There Clavigo
alighted and walked to the center of the
square, which was lined with troops on
three sides. The captain, when he reached
the required position, bandaged his own
eyes and then again bowed to the people.


The officer in command of the firing
squad then gave the order to fire and
Clavigo fell.


LONDON, ENG, June "a dispatch
from Madrid says that the soldiers who exc
cuted Clavigo had to fire at him three
times. Clavigo first fell with three bullets
in his head, and he still moved after a SOL
der had fired another shot into his head
from under the chin. He did not die until
another soldier fired bullet through his
heart. The scene caused great excitement
among the Mortified spectators.

by four men to rob Farmer Adam Kas, re-
siding near the southwest corner OF Fort
Crook, which resulted in the fatally shoot
ing of Adam Kas Jr. and the serious
wonnding of his father


Three men stepped on the porch of the
Kas residence and asked for young Kas.
The father asked what was wanted, as the
boy was sleeping in the barn. and was in
formed that they had horses which they
wanted to put in the barn until morning.


He ran to a rear room in the house and
called to his daughter, servant and hired
man, who sleep upstairs, and the men
broke down the door and followed him.
One of the burglars held Kas Sr., the sec
ond beat him on the head with revolver,
while the third stood guard over the hired
man and the two women of the house.


Kas fought his way out of the house to
the front porch, when one of the men
knocked him down. Young Kas then ap-
peared upon the scene, and seeing that one
OF the men was beating his father, placed
a revolver to the robbers head and fred.
The fellow got to his feet and Kas shot at
him the second time, and the fellow fell
from the porch. Before be could shoot the
third time Kas was shot twice in the back,
and fell, when one Of the men stepped up
to him and placed his revolver below his
left ear and fired. The bullet passed
through his head and came out below the
right eye. Vic McCarty and his gang are
under arrest for the crime.

TACOMA, WASH, May 16.-Large forest
fires are raging along both sides of the
Northern Pacific tracks from South Prairie
to the summit of the Cascade Mountains, a
distance of fifty-fve miles. At Lester,
seventy miles east of here. the postoffice
building and two small residences were
burned with all their contents yesterday.
The railroad employees saved the COM
panys property by using locomotives and
throwing water over the buildings. There
were number of loaded trains on the side
tracks there. The fire caught from burn
ing logs and is still raging about the town.
The railroads bridge and section crews are
all fighting the flames. Superintendent
McCabe reports that fires were put out in
the snowsheds several times to-day. They
had caught from falling burning trees. A
high wind would cause great damage, but
rain is looked for.

ASBURY PARK, n. J., July 9.-The
second day of the National League of
American Wheelmen meet here proved
most enjoyable. The weather could not
have been fairer or the roads in better con-
dition. Hundreds of cyclers from every
section of the Union, Canada and even Eu-
rope arrived with wheels and gay badges
on every train; bands played marches and
the register of visitors at the clubhouse of
the Asbury Park Wheelmen fairly buIged
out with its host of entries, while the
seemingly inexhaustible supply of creden-
tial buttons waxed lower and lower in the
committeeman desks.


Following close upon the Denver, Pitts
burg and Harrisburg contingents, which
arrived yesterday, came large delegations
of the Chicago Cycle Club, Pennsylvania
Wheelmen, Time Wheelmen, Century
Wheelmen and Press Cycle Club ri Phila-
delphia.


The only Arthur Augustus Zimmerman,
looking like typical Jersey farmer, and
his side partner, Harry Wheeler, took the
Denver men in tow last night and prone
naded them about town and over the beach
until the travel-sore hearts of the Rocky
Mountain men were faint and their shoes
were full of sand, but with no disccuraging
effect upon their irrepressible lungs and
wild Western yells.


To-day the only excitements have been
the run to Long Branch, through the Inter
laken and Elberon, by the famous Surf
road, the great parade and the discussion
of Miss Kittie Knox's case. She is an ex-
tremely comely colored girl from Boston,
who recently won the first prize in the
Maiden cycle parade for wearing the most
tasteful and artistic woman's wheeling
garb. When Miss Knox, whose appearance
and dress had been objects of admiration
all day, walked into the committee-room
at the local clubhouse and presented her
league card for credential badge the gen.
tleman in charge refused to recognize the
card, and the young woman withdrew very
quietly.


Then the discussion commenced. Ninety
nine out of every hundred members inter
viewed express the heartiest sympathy for
her and condemnation OF the hasty action
OF the badge committee. The first vice
president of the i. A. W., G. A. Perkins of
Boston, said to-day that he considered the
refusal entirely unwarranted.


The great parade was reviewed at the
league headquarters in the Ocean Hotel by
Vice President Perkins, Secretary and
Treasurer Van Mort of the Pennsylvania
division, Frederick Gerlach, George K.
Barrett, w. Montague Perrett and F. J..
Wagner of Chicago, E. G. Bode of Cleve-
land, Andry o. McGarritt of Boston, G. A.
Limon of Philadeinhia and Chief Counsel
Gentle of the New Jersey division, who
acts as one of the judges to award prizes
for the Clubs parading the largest delega-
ton and the organization making the
finest appearance.


The principal thoroughfares were lined
with citizens, visitors and excursionists,
beauty. The Denver Wheel Club carried
first prize for both numbers and appear
ance, parading fifty-four men and women,
all attired in spotless white linen suits and
yachting caps. The second prize went to
the keystone Wheelmen of Philadelphia
and the third to the Mercer Wheelmen
Club of Trenton. The clubs prominent in
the line were the Pennsylvania Bicycle
Club, Time Wheelmen, Quaker City Wheel
men and Pennsylvania Wheelmen of Phil
adelphia, the Harrisburg Wheel Club, Nc
Keesport Wheelmen and the Portsmouth
(Va.l Wheel Club.


The ladies division, led by Mrs. Bough-
ton of New York, showed fifty-seven
women, thirty-three of whom wore the
bloomer costume, ten short skirts and the
remainder the conventional habit.

SALT LAKE, UTAH, April 21.-The mys-
terry surrounding the disappearance of
three young men who lived in the vicinity
of Utah Lake, near Lehi, Utah, is gradually
being cleared up.


Albert Hayes, Andrew Johnson and AL
fred Nelson, had been living near
Pelican Point for some time, but were
| elected about two months ago on a suit
| brought by Oliver A. Slade. The mer


were missed some time ago, and on Mon
day last the body of Hayes was found neal
| the lake shore. Death had been caused by
| two gunshot wounds. Late yesterday aft
ernoon the bodies of Johnson and Nelson
| were found. They were discovered in the
lake, on wagon and were tied down with


ropes.


| The bodies presented sickening ap-


pearance. The murders probably occurred
| in February. The murdered men were all
cousins and were running a stock business


on the ranch.


| The theory is that the men were mur-


dered in the cabin during the night and
thrown into the lake, as the bodies were


partly undressed when found. The gun


shot wounds appear to have been made
with 44-caliber rifle.


Suspicion, it is said, points to III. Hayes,
the stepfather of one of the murdered men,
and son of his who is missing. Other
theories are advanced, but have no motive
to support them.


The country surrounding the ranch is


wild and broken, and has been the scene
of many tragedies between the Indians
and early settlers.


The Coroner's jury examined the bodies
to-day and will continue the investigation
at Lehi tomorrow. The excitement runs
high, especially among ranchmen in the
vicinity of the murders. Some arrests are
expected tomorrow.
