SACRAMENTO, CAL, July 13.-All day


the great building of the electric company


has echoed with the hum and rattle of ma


chinery driven with inconceivable rapidity
by the resistless and magical power that


generated at Folsom, has travelled with the
ripidity of thought over the long lines of
copper that stretch their way through the
fertile fields of the broad Sacramento Val
ley. All day have skilled artisans in the


employ of the company carefully watched


every movement of that machinery, tight


ened bolt here and relaxed another in
some other portion, until the whole ran


with nicely and precision.


At half past o'clock this morning word


was received from the electric power-house
| at Folsom that the new quadrant had been
| fitted to the governor and all was in


readiness to start the huge turbine wheels
into life and motion, and orders were i'm


mediately given to go ahead.


| The power arrived almost instantly and


heralded It's advent by smashing two in


candescent lights. These were soon re-


placed, and in an instant the entire row


shone with great brilliancy.
Chief Engineer Blackwell of the General
Electric Company walked to the switch
| board, while Resident Engineer Lighthipe
stationed himself by the side of the


massive motor.


care You ready?" demanded the chief


engineer, as he laid his hands upon the
brass handles of the switch?


| LET her come" was the reply.
| There was quick movement of the


hands, and instantly the building was
| filled with a vast buzzing sound, as
| ! - l.
been overturned at once, but the motor
failed to start.


stop her." cried Lighthipe, and the


noise ceased.


AS the handles on the switchboard were
| thrown up several men grasped the


fange of the shaft of the huge motor and


again the current was thrown on.
| AS the buzzing sound rang out the men


exerted their strength to aid the current,


the motor groaned slightly, then slowly
| started, and the next moment was spin
| ming around with inconceivable rapidity.
"She's off she's off," rang from
| mouth to mouth of the excited crowd of
| spectators grouped around the machine,
and the Duzzing noise of the machinery
| changed to roar and rattle that sounded
| far on the chill night air.


| There came sharp, loud explosion that
caused all the uninitiated to Jump, and the


next instant the room was filled with bril-
| liant lightning flashes that lit the entire
| structure with its lurid CLEANS. The ex-
| plosion was closely followed by another,


and the brilliant flashes of light almost
caused stampede of spectators for the
outer air. But the engineers who have


made life study of the antics of the cleo
trio fluid simply smiled, cut off the cur


rent and informed the startled crowd that
two safety fuses had blown out within a
| few brief moments. They were replaced,
| and again the rattle of machinery rang
out.


| Shortly afterward the connecting clutch


was thrown into gear and the entire line


of shafting began rapidly to revolve. Faster
and faster it spun, while on all sides could
be heard expressions of delight. Superin-
tendent Shock warmly grasped the hand
OF Foreman Francis, Workmen fairly en-
braced their fellows with as much warmth
as an eager youth salutes the idol of his
dreams, while one excited individual loudly


shouted: "See old Betsy! Hear her hunt


Amt she daisy?" referring to the motor.
Then one of the workmen ran to where
superintendent Shock was standing, put
an excited query, received an affirmative
answer, and, followed by a number of
others, rushed from the building, to return
after brief absence bearing in their arms,
with infinite care, the recllning-chair con-
tanning their injured comrade, who had
had his leg crushed by the rolling of a
shaft TIE preceding week. He had waited
fully attired in his nearby home for the
glad tidings that meant to Sacramento
that new era had dawned; that
the old city by the rushing river
leading to the ocean and the foreign marts
of commerce would be merged and lost in
the great manufacturing center of the flu
ture. The invalid's face fairly shone with
happiness as he watched the rapidly NOV
ing machinery and his pains and weari-
ness were forgotten.


For over two hours the machinery was
allowed to pursue its rapid course, and the
glad news was announced TO the slumber-
ing city by the loud roar of cannon. Re-
port followed report until 100 guns had
echoed through its length and startled
sleepers realized the success of the stu
pendous enterprise.

HEALDSBURG, CAL, Aug. 29.-There
is lively scrimmage for wine grapes in
Sonoma County this season, and the
grape-grower sits by, while buyers hunt
him up to treat for his vintage.


Last season at this time producers were
in the dumps. No one wanted grapes, or
if they did, SIS to 81 per ton were the ruling
figures, and even at these prices from sixty
days to six months time was given in
which to pay for the grapes.


With $4,000 tons of grapes ripening on
the vines and the wine-making time only
two weeks away. many of the vineyardists
have not yet sold. They are not uneasy,
however, for the buyer wants them and
will pay $40 to S13 ton spot cash.


The new wineries that have been built
the past season and the old ones enlarged
have increased the capacity nearly mil.
lion gallons. Then, too, nearly all the dry
wines of the county have been shipped out,
and as result cooperage is empty. The
manufacturer desires to fill his cellar ca
pacity, and those who are inactive will
fail, for the grape crop is notaup to the
average, and many tanks will remain
empty.


The wine-makers' corporation has the
call on grapes, for while those outside the
compact are offering slight advance on
syndicate prices the producer is staying
with the winemen, who have banded to-
gether for the betterment of the industry.

to come to Denver.


1t was delightfully."- warm Indian sum-
mer day. The route of the parade was
long one, and fully 100, 900 people witnessed
the display. Governor McIntire and his
staff, accompanied by Brigadier- General
Wheaton and staff Of the Department of
the Colorado, reviewed the pageant from
mammoth grand stand located on Broad
way, opposite to which living flag COM
posed of school children made pictures
que sight.


The pageant was designed to show the
progress made by Colorado and was an
historical review, beginning with float
representing prehistoric cliff-dwellers and
ending with a parade of school children
carrying flowers, fruit and grain in sheaves.
The most interesting portions of the pa
geant were the bands OF Ute and Santa
Clara Indians on horseback, all decked in
their holiday attire of paint, feathers and
beaded buckskin suits. They were in
charge of Colonel Cooper who has been
recently elected member of their tribe,
and old Chief Savaro. A brass band from
the Teller Institute, Government Indian
school, with float exhibiting the handi
work OF that school, showed what progress
the Indians have been making.


Following the Indians were the mem bers
OF the Colorado Pioneer Society in old
Concord stagecoaches and canvas-topped
wagons drawn by OK teams, mule teams
and old horses. At the head of this divi-
sion rode old Jim Baker, the oldest trapper
and Indian scout now living, who crossed
the plains in 1888 with party sent out by
the American Fur Company. In this dIvi-
sion also were number of gaudily attired
Mexican riders from Southern Colorado
headed by Senator Barela of Trinidad.


Floats representing pioneer gambling
saloon. the first printing office in Denver,
the first church, the finding of gold on
Cherry Creek; floats showing mounted
wild animals. and beautiful allegorical
floats representing Colorado's mineral re-
sources, added to the picturesqueness of
the parade.


Cripple Creek contributed a number of
magnificent floats. The agricultural and
horticultural resources and the fruits of
irrigation were represented appropriately,
and the firms manufacturing Colorado ma
terials into useful products were out with
admirably executed floats. There were
twenty-five bands in the parade, including
the famous Cowboy band, now located in
Cripple Creek.


After the parade had ended the floats
were taken to the city park where they
will remain as an outdoor State fair until
the festival ends. In the park also are the
camps of the Indians and the two regi-
ments of the Colorado National Guards.


Tonight a trolley musicale was given,
bands occupying ten brightly Illuminated
cars which moved slowly through the busi-
ness streets and stopped at stations desig-
mated by the festival committee to give
open-air concerts to the crowds.


The second days programme consists of
military parade in the morning, with
the United States troops and cavalry from
Fort Logan and the two regiments of the
Colorado National Guards as the principal
features, and will include all military and
semi-military societies. In the afternoon
prize drills occur at the park and exhibit
tion drills by the United States troops.

from Southern Ohio, Southeastern Indiana
and Northeastern Kentucky report phe-
nomenal waterspouts before sunset last
night. At McGonigle's Station, near
Hamilton, crops were badly damaged, as
also were bridges and fences. In Scioto
County the people were greatly alarmed.

ton.

waterspout inundated the country.
Water was three feet deep in the fields,
carrying logs and fencing into the high
ways. Trees were blown down and toll

damaged. In none of the localities did the
damage extend beyond mile square.

to-day between Torrent and Fincastle,
Kentucky, causing a big landslide. The
North Fork of the Kentucky River rose
three feet in one hour.

STOCKTON, CAL, April 29.-Judge
Smith to-day decided the insurance suits
brought by the Stockton Combined Har-
vester and Agricultural works against the
Glenns Falls and other insurance COM
panies, giving Judgment for the plaintiff.


In rendering the decision Judge Smith
said that the insurance com panies had in
sured the property of the plaintiff for
$4,000 and that subsequently this prop
erty had been entirely destroyed by fire.
This amount of insurance was made with
a full knowledge of the value and condi-
ton of the property insured. After
this fire the defendants agreed to pay
$4,000 for the losses sustained after a
careful examination into the extent of
the losses suffered by the plaintiff.
The Judge held that the answer and cross
complaint were not sustained and directed
that judgment and order for the plain
tiffs be entered. The court remarked that
the company had made certain agreements
and that no good cause had been shown
why these should not have been carried
out.


This suit involves some thirteen leading
fire insurance companies and was stub
bornly fought by them, Attorneys T. G.
Van Ness and Budd & Budd appearing for
the defendants. The first trial occupied
forty-eight days and was won by the plant
iff, but on an appeal to the Supreme Court
the action was remanded for a rehearing.

WAGNER, Ind. T., Aug. 1.-With the
exception of ten. the gang of Indians who
have committed series of diabolical
crimes since July 30 in the Territory, were
captured near Okmulgee last Thursday
started for the Fort Smith (Ark.) jail to
avoid being lynched.


News has been received here that mob
of Muskogee citizens has gone across the
country to Fort Gibson to intercept the
Missouri Pacific train carrying the mis-
creants and their captors, for the purpose
of dealing out summary justice.


The gang. which began its heinons opera
tions by numbering Deputy United States
Marshal John Garratt at Okmulgee and
escaping over the hills to the Greek Nation,
was led by Rufus Buck, a Uche Indian.
His followers were Samuel Sampson,
Meorna July, Bub Lucky, alias Lucky
Davis; Albert Stake and Levy Davis. The
day after numbering Garratt, the gang met
a white man and his daughter in wagon.
Covering the man with their guns, the In
dians took the girl from the wagon. Their
next victims were Ben Callahan and a
negro boy. whom the gang met on the
road. They murdered the boy and beat
Callahan so that they believed him to be
dead when they left the scene after robbing
the man of money, boots and saddle.


At the country stores of West and ].
Norrburg at Orket, the murderers and rob-
bers held up the owners and took away
everything they could carry, Next in their
path of crime they met two white women
and girl IA years old, and murder was
again added to their list.

Baltimore and Ohio train brought

body of James Settle, a sixteen-year-
old boy, who had been killed by the
train at Point Mills. The boy spent last
night with party of friends in the woods
and got but little sleep. When he came
home this morning he drove the cows to
pasture, accompanied by a big shepherd
dog: He was drowsy, and on the way
back sat down on the track to rest the
dog lying beside hom.


Engineer Henry McBirney says that when
the train rounded the curve beyond the
Point Mills cut he saw the boy lying full
length along the rail. The dog, knowing
the danger, had seized his coat collar and
was tugging with all his might, having
his feet planted just outside the rail, try
ing to Pull his masters body off the track
The train was near that 1t could not
be stopped. but the air was put on and the
speed checked. while the whistle was
footed.


The boy was partially awakened by the
dogs efforts and began beating the faithful
brute with his fist, but the dog held on
and put forth all his power to save his
master. AS the engine drew nearer McBir-
ney and the fireman shut their eyes to
hide the death scene from their view
When the train was stopped and run back
both the boy and his constant companion
were found horribly mangled.

ROME, ITALY, Nov. This city was
visited by violent earthquake at $40
o'clock this morning. People were aroused
from sleep and fled to the open squares.
The greatest CONSERVATION prevailed.


The Convent Santa Maria Maggiore was
greatly damaged. The outer wall was
overthrown and the ceiling has fallen.
One of its inmates. a monk, was injured.


The shocks were confined to the province
of Rome. Official observatory reports say
that the first manifestations were a slight
bling that lasted about five seconds.
These became more violent for a period of
eight seconds, and then became slighter
for nine seconds. The direction of the
movements was north to south.


The shocks created great panic among
the inmates of the prison and mutiny
was attempted, but was quickly suppressed
by troops and order restored.


The Pope was awakened by the shocks.
He remained perfectly calm. After rising
he made haste to inquire the news from
the city.


Investigation has disclosed the fact that
the damage done was much greater than
at first supposed. Four palaces and the
Bank of Italy were go shaken that they
are unsafe. The Palazzo Odeschalchi, one
of the finest in Rome, and five other
structures of that character also were
seriously damaged. The building of the
Ministry of Finance was slightly damaged.

SAN DIEGO, CAL, May 2o.-A remarka-

Schultz, the well-known marine and land
scape artist, with two young companions,


L. Foster and John William keenan,.
They left here March 2S and have spent
the intervening time in a five weeks trip
down the Colorado River, Schultz in quest
of striking landscapes and the young fell
lows IN search of adventure. ALI got more

ten feet higher than usual ON account of
melting SHOWS.


They went above Needles, made boat,
stocked it with provisions and started
boldly down the river. None had much
experience in shooting the rapids, but they
are now veterans in the business. They
made their way quite well the first day,

their companion all the way to Yuma.
| One of the first dangerous experiences

| Following the current, the boat swept

| The next exciting experience was in Red


Canyon, where the mad waters had cut an


immense cave in the solid rock wall, in


which a whirlpool gathered trees, snags


and the boat with its three occupants.


There similar fight was made, with SIM
| liar result. After reaching smooth water


the boat was run to the bank and keenan,


jumped ashore to make fast. The treach-


erous bank, though bearing big trees and


apparently solid, gave way, and the young


fellow fell into the deep water, almost
uEOWnlHg DeIoTe OCuulZ anu OSIer

| Schultz said the river was treacherous


above any other quality. There is an i'm
mense quantity of soluble matter in the


water, and the constantly changing chan


mel made the work of irrigation uncertain,


and Schultz predicts that the mouth of the


great canal now under construction to irri-
| gate the Colorado Desert will be choked

During the trip the voyagers found a

north, which were correct though they re-

torian.

reach of known mythologies naturally fell
q prey to the absurdities of medieval and

PHILADELPHIA, Pa, July 21.-A
pleasant days outing in Paramount Park
had tragic termination this evening.


AS Edward Scallin, his wife and five
children were crossing the driveway at the
Poplar street entrance to the park, run
away horse, attached to light buggy, in
which was seated woman Juggling fran
tically at the reins, dashed down upon the
little family group and trampled under
foot two of the children, Nellie, aged 10,
and Joseph, aged Z. The buggy passed
over the PROSTATE bodies of the two chill
dren. and when the terror-stricken parents
lifted their little ones from the ground the
boy was dead and the girl unconscious.
The injured child was taken to the hospi-
tai, where an examination showed that
she had received fracture of the skull and
thigh and leg. The injuries will probably
result fatally.


What became of the horse and the woman
who was In the buggy is not known. The
frightened animal continued on its way
after trampIing the children under hoof
and disappeared. The police tonight re-
ported that they stopped runaway horse
at Twenty -fourth and Green streets, but
beyond this they knew nothing about the
runaway.

of the saddest events recorded in the
county was the burning to death, near
Azusa, of little three-year-old Marion Mil
lar and the suicide of her father in conse-
quence.


The Millars lived about three miles from
Azusa on ranch. The family consisted
of Millar, wife and two daughters, one
aged %, the other 3 years old. Millar was
especially devoted to the youngest child.
Last Wednesday afternoon, while only
these two were in the house. Millar fell
asleep, and during his slHmber the child
possessed herself of some matches and set
fire TO her dress.


The eldest daughter on returning home
discovered the body of the little one,
frightfully burned and blistered, near
where the father was still sleeping. She
awoke him, and he was so overcome by
grief that he took his rifle, went out into
the yard and sent bullet through his
brain. He is dying, and the shock of the
two fatalities has completely Frustrated

DENVER. Oct. 16.-Today's inaugura
tion of the Festival of Mountain and
Plain was an immense success IN every
way. Not only did the big pageant of
progress far surpass the expectations even
of the carnival management themselves,
but the crowd of visitors from outside
towns exceeded any ever witnessed in
Denver.


The parade. from every standpoint, out
ranks anything of the kind ever seen in
the west. Each OF the five divisions was
a parade in itself, and altogether it made
a parade ovtr .hree miles long, which was
an hour and a half in passing given
point


Pioneers ana floats, representing the
advancement of Colorado from the time
Of the cliff dwellers. to today came first.
Every float was a feature, many of them
being genuine works OF art, in the prep
aration of which no expense had been
spared. The galy attired bands of In
dians attracted more attention, perhaps.
than anything else, though old Jim
Baker the squaw man who trapped and
hunted through these regions sixty years
ago, was everywhere enthusiastically
cheered. He rode horse that crossed
the plains in 1859.


1t was in the second division, repre.
senting the mineral wealth of the state,
that the most gorgeous effect was seen.
Cripple Creek and Leadville excelled all
othere. their floats truly representing the
marvellous richness of their respective
camps. Agriculture, horticulture and live
stock came next. Mesa and Montrose
counties making the best displays, closely
rivaled by Fremont and other counties.
Manufactures of Denver had the next
division, doing themselves proud in the
matter of their displays. The disting-
uished citizens who havs been most
prominent in building the state consti-
tuted the fourth division the parade,
while the last was devoted TO the various
civic societies, in which the old timers
came in for a share of praise. Tonight
the tramway company ran a dozen illu-
minated cars over their lines in the busi
ness section. Colored electric lights made
them literally solid mass OF light. The
street decorations excel even those of the
conclave. Sixteenth street is festooned
with 1000 electric lights and nearly all
of the principal business houses are illu-
minated.


Tonight the city was illuminated, over
1000 electric lights being used on Six
teenth stree from Larimer to Broadway.
The dozens of Bands visiting the local,
were all playing and music Iesounded
from every street corner, while trains of
tramway cars, literally covered with col
ored electric lights, tfaversed the various
street car lines.

text:
SIMLA, INDIA, April THE First Bri'
gade of the British forces moving to the re-
lief of Mr.. Robertson, the British agent at
Chitral, had an engagement with 5000
Swatis, who were trying to block the Mala-
kand Pass. The enemy were put to fight
after losing thirty killed by charge OF cav
airy. The brigade is now at Khar, in
Swat, where it is awaiting the organiza-
ton of transport service.


A considerable number of fanatics from
Upper Swat have joined Umra Khan of
Jandol, who is leading the forces against
the British, and big fight is expected to-
morrow.


Further advices received from the
front state that the British have
crossed the Swat River and captured Thana,
Umra Khan's fort The Eleventh Bengal
Lancers charged force commanded by
Umra Khan's brother. The enemy lost
100 men. The British casualties were
slight.


The enemy stoutly resisted the British
attempts to throw pontoons across the
Swat River this morning. The Swatis oc-
cupied the routes commanding the river,
and kept up continual fire on the engi-
neers and others employed in placing pom
toons - position.


Brigadier- General Waterford's brigade,
with the Fifty-sixth regiment, advanced
and forced passage of the river, assisted
by mounted battery and a Maxim gun.
Then the Eleventh Bengal Lancers made
brilliant dash and crossed the river. They
at once attacked the enemy, who retreated.
The lancers pursued them to Uck, killing
100 of them.


The Fourth and Fifteenth regiments
then crossed the river and occupied Chalk
rama.


The Scottish Borderers forded the river
at point mile distant from where the
pontoon bridge was placed and captured
Thana with little trouble. The British
loss was one sapper and a few other men
killed. A number of horses were also
killed. A thousand camels with the trans
port train have succeeded in crossing the
Mainland Pass and have arrived at Kahr.

Four Chinese arrested at Chicago Under


the EccIusfOn Act.


CHICAGO, ILL.,, Sept. 4.-Four China
man, Lee zee, Lee Quong, Lee Joe and
Lee Yung, who were arrested several
weeks ago in Detroit under the exclusion
act, were found guilty of conspiring to
smuggle themselves into this country and
sentenced to ten days in the Detroit work
house at hard labor and then to deporta-
ton. They were brought to this city en-
route to the Pacific Coast and stopped by a
writ of habeas corpus.


The position taken by the counsel for the
prisoners was that the order of deportation
was void because the Commissioner had
imposed sentence of imprisonment.
Judge Seaman of the United States Circuit
Court to-day held that the Commissioner
had exceeded his power in assessing the
imprisonment, which rendered his iudg-
ment void, and he ordered the four men
released.


Special Treasury Agent Grain swore out
another complaint charging the four men
with violation of the exclusion act, and
they furnished bonds in the sum of $4,000
each. The attorneys for the four men,
who may decide to test the law, say no
complication will arise before the Commits
sioner, as they will prove the men are
members of Chicago business houses.

The storm that ragged off the Oregon
coast must have been a very heavy one,
for almost every vessel that arrives has a
tale OF disaster to tell. The Topgallant
headed the list with the loss of her deck
load ana her bow stove in, but vessels that
have arrived since have reported very
rough experience. The Spartan and Lou
isiana both had their cargoes shifted, and
the America, which got in last night, had
similar experience.


Some of the men on the schooner Me-
lancthon had narrow escape during the
run from Grays Harbor to San Francisco.
When off the Colum bia River the storm
ives at its worst. Antoine Johnson was at
the wheel and Chris Smith standing near
the mainmast, when big cross-sea came
CURING aboard. Johnson yelled to the
men to hold on, and he himself took a firm
grip on the spokes of the wheel. The sea
took almost everything movable overheard.
The spanker boom was broken and the
pinnacle and compass went by the board.
The captain had a small compass attached
to his watch-chain, and by it the schooner
was navigated to San Francisco.


II have been sailing up and down this
coast for twenty years" said Johnson yes
terday, land | have never encountered
such sea- There were a succession of
gales from the southeast and southwest,
which raised an immense cross-sea and
kept our decks flooded all the time.


When the big wave broke aboard Smith
was standing near the mainmast and that
was the last l saw of him until after the
deck was clear. Then saw Smith stand
ing on his head. with his legs over the
starboard rail. Some of the boys ran out
and got him into the forecastIe before
another sea broke aboard. He was almost
dead and 1t was some time before he was
brought around"


Besides breaking her spanker- boom and
losing the pinnacle and compass the Me-
lancthon lost the greater portion of her
rail- 1t will cost over $500 to put her in
thorough seas going order again.,


The America was fourteen days making
the run from Departure Bay, but only
eight DAYS from Port Angeles. On account
OF the heavy weather prevailing along the
coast the captain anchored for several days
at the latter place. Once past Flattery,
however, the southeast to southwest gales
reported by other vessels were encoun-
tered and the America had a hard battle
OF it. Off the Columbia River, the cargo
shlfted and the vessel had to be put before
the wind IN order to repair damages.


While none of the coasting feet are over
DUE still the owners are feeling very anx-
lous on account Of the stories of heavy
weather brought in by each new arrival.

Gustaf Broman, who is to ride his cedar
log canoe around the world, going via
Cape Horn if the railroad will not haul
him overland to New York for start on
his voyage arrived by the Arcata. The
bold navigator did not sail down in his
boat, but stood safely on the steamer and
watched the clumsy dugout drag at it's
towline like pile.


The craft is fitted with contrivances
never before seen on land or sea. and hav-
ing more depth than beam, is about as safe
for passenger service as bale Of hay.


Not content with the natural crankiness
consequent upon its unshiplike construc-
ton the architect has riveted brass chain,
plates and other heavy articles to the rail
and deck, which further raises her center
of gravity, making her an elegant and
graceful capsizer.


Captain Broman had his boat loaded on
a truck and conveyed up town for repairs.
1t is safe to say that the bold navigator
will navigate his uncanny and uninterest-
ing craft into some fake museum, and it
will be proven that she was designed not
for ocean travel, but for the Midway nickel
trade.

The police Of the East One Hundred
and Twenty-ffth street station have no
trace yet of the brutal burglar who
nearly choked to death Mrs. Barbara
Klein. of 341 East One Hundred and
Seventeenth street, after robbing her
nat Of her hard-earned savings. last
Tuesday afternoon.


The Kleins live on the first floor. in
the rear. in two rooms. which the wife
keeps scrupulously clean. She had been
out washing Tuesday afternoon. When
she returned and stepped into the
kitchen she was seized by the burglar
and choked into insensibility.


The ruffian then clapped a sponge
saturated with chloroform over the
woman's mouth and left. locking the
door from the outside.


Mrs. Klein lay unconscious for over
an hour before her neighbors suspected
anything. One of them went to the
door and raped repeatedly without re-
ceiving any answer. Finally, discover
ing that there was a key in the lock,
which the burglar had failed to remove
in his haste. the neighbor unlocked the
door and was shocked to see Mrs. Klein
lying PROSTATE on the floor apparently
Nfeless.


A doctor was summoned and the
neighbors revived the woman. She
vomited blood at every attempt to arise.
and the doctor said she had narrowly
escaped death.


Mrs. Klein Is twenty-six years old and
her husband. Frank. is twenty eight
Seven months ago they came to this
country from Germany in the hope of
making a better living for themselves.


To add to his meagre income the wife
cheerfully volunteered to take in wash
ing and by constant drudging the couple
at the end OF six weeks had saved
enough money to send to Germany for
their boy. who was to sail with a
friend. Then the little girl died and the
boys coming was deferred.


The couple had about made up the ex-
penses of the funeral again and Mrs
Klein had saved eight of the ten dollars
towards paying for the boys passage to
New York. Another friend to sail next
month. promised to bring the boy along.


All this money the burglar took with
him and the parents are nearly heart
broken. The sons coming must again
be postponed unless some charitably in
clined persons come to the aid OF the
distressed father and mother.

HEALDSBURG, CAL, July 3.-The sur
veying party that has for the past several
weeks been laying out the route for the
proposed railroad from this city through
the Dry Creek Valley and up into the big
redwood belt, along the Mendocino coast,
is camped in Dry Creek Valley, three miles
above town, and will probably run the
lines into Healdsburg on Friday. The
survey is completed to within four miles
of town, and the distance covered by the
surveyors is III miles.


Members of the surveying party claim
that Chicago capitalists would build the
road, but many here believe that the
Southern Pacific is behind the move
and that the Santa Rosa branch
of that road will be extended to
Healdsburg and on up the route surveyed.
The country through which the surveyors
have been working emb races the rich Dry
Creek Valley, through which the road
runs for twenty miles, thence into the
Anderson Valley in Mendocino County,
terminating in a redwood belt OF great ex-
tent.


The effect of the work already done has
caused Dry Greek farm property to take
an advance, and several farms have
changed hands recently at high figures.
The extension of the Southern Pacific
branch to this city would prove an in
calculable benefit to cannery men and
wine merchants who could then load cars
direct for Eastern shipment.
